# Compost pile management

Composting depends on microbes breaking down mixed plant material, and their diet needs a rough balance of carbon-rich browns such as dry leaves and cardboard with nitrogen-rich greens such as kitchen scraps and fresh clippings. A pile of only greens turns dense and sour; only browns barely heats up. A starting ratio around two or three parts brown material by volume to one part green keeps decomposition active.

Moisture should feel like a wrung-out sponge: damp throughout but never dripping. Turning the pile every week or two reintroduces oxygen; a heap that sits compacted goes anaerobic, smells rotten and stalls. A working pile warms noticeably in its center, sometimes steaming on a cold morning, then cools as the material matures.

The balance matters beyond the pile itself. Soil microbes decomposing high-carbon residues like fresh wood chips pull nitrogen from the surrounding soil to build their own cells, temporarily starving nearby plants — mulch keeps chips on the surface so the tie-up stays out of the root zone. Finished compost is dark, crumbly and earthy smelling, with the original ingredients no longer recognizable. Keep out meat, dairy and greasy food, which attract rodents, and never compost diseased foliage, since home piles rarely stay hot enough to kill the pathogens inside.
